strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem: seam cutting cannot hide every residual alignment error. Repairing only problematic seam neighborhoods is a sensible, potentially useful contribution, and fixing boundary labels provides a clear mechanism for reconnecting local and global seams.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. For example, baseline SSIM increases from 0.638 to 0.696 on SEAGULL, with corresponding improvements in RMSE, PSNR, and ZNCC.
Figures 1, 3, and 6 provide convincing examples of reduced structural discontinuities. The pipeline illustration and pseudocode make the overall approach accessible.

The manuscript cites its main algorithmic components and public datasets, provides a code/data link, and reports key parameter settings and hardware. Its explicit discussion of failed detection and patch-boundary artifacts is informative.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily an integration of established techniques, and its advantage over closely related seam-guided alignment approaches is insufficiently established. Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a single qualitative comparison in Fig. 6; the cited dense-matching seam/warp approach [21] is not evaluated. Quantitative comparisons with relevant joint alignment/seam methods would better establish the contribution's significance.

The central flow modification is underspecified. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Eq. (5) defines a scalar sigmoid whose argument is subsequently described as a normalized spatial coordinate. The intended spatial weighting of the displacement, its orientation, and its treatment of all patch boundaries need explicit definitions. The sigmoid also does not exactly attain the stated endpoint values. These are consequential reproducibility ambiguities, although potentially correctable.

The quantitative evidence primarily measures inter-image agreement around the resulting seam. These metrics support improved local matching but do not establish preservation of scene geometry or perceptual quality throughout the mosaic. Representative visual examples help, but a systematic assessment of final-image artifacts, structural distortion, or human preference is missing. Dataset averages also conceal how frequently individual results deteriorate.

There are no quantitative ablations establishing the roles of patch selection, sigmoid modulation, and boundary constraints; Fig. 3 supplies only an illustrative parameter comparison. The threshold max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) can accept uniformly poor seams, while small patches can introduce distortion, as acknowledged in Fig. 7. The frequency of these failures and sensitivity to the parameters remain unmeasured, leaving the method's operating range uncertain.

The efficiency claim has limited comparative support. Table III reports approximately 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, often exceeding the original seam-cutting time. Initial alignment is excluded, image resolutions are not specified, and no comparable runtime measurements are provided for Parallax or SEAGULL. Consequently, the claimed practical advantage over those alternatives is not demonstrated.
